newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels warn army officers to surrender.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels warn army officers to surrender.

text.p: plans, pvs Kinshasa)
By Matthew Tostevin
Zairean rebels warned army officers on Wednesday to lay down their arms as regional leaders, including Zaire's beleaguered prime minister, gathered for talks in Nairobi on the crisis.
At rebel headquarters in Goma, Voice of the People radio said army officers who failed to lay down their arms before rebels arrived would be charged with "high treason and rebellion".
It said officers should leave their guns at Zaire's second largest city of Lubumbashi in the southern mineral-rich region of Shaba or at Kikwit, 500 km (300 miles) east of the capital.

In Nairobi, African presidents gathered for a meeting on the deepening crisis. Their gathering followed by one day a disputed Zairean parliament vote calling for the sacking of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who represented his government at the Kenya talks.

Supporters of Kengo and ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko said the vote was flawed because too few transitional parliament members took part. But opposition militants planned to demonstrate on Wednesday in the capital in support of the vote.

"I am not aware (of) any changes in the government of Zaire. The summit is still on. Perhaps we will know more when the prime minister himself arrives at State House," said a Kenyan official, referring to the venue for the talks.

Kengo's presence ends a Zairean government boycott of two previous rounds of talks on Zaire in Nairobi. The rebels were not invited and argue Kenya's President Daniel arap Moi only wants to prop up Mobutu.

Kenyan officials said Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe, Congolese President Pascal Lissouba, South African Deputy President Thabo Mbeki and President Paul Biya of Cameroon were due to arrive on Wednesday for the meeting called by Moi.
But diplomats, speaking even before the parliamentary vote against Kengo, expected little progress without representatives of the rebels and their allies Uganda and Rwanda.
Mobutu, 66 and Zaire's ruler for 32 years, was invited but is being treated for cancer in Monte Carlo and has remained in Europe most of the time since the revolt began last October.

Kenya, South Africa, Zimbabwe and Cameroon were mandated by a "Nairobi Two" summit last December to lead African efforts to end the fighting in Zaire -- where rebels have captured a fifth of the territory including the city of Kisangani at the weekend.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila declared a ceasefire around the captured city of Kisangani from Tuesday and said Kinshasa and diamond mining hub of Mbuji-Mayi in Kasai were his next targets.
The Zairean radical opposition in Kinshasa led by Etienne Tshisekedi sponsored Tuesday's parliamentary motion of censure, which also called for a ceasefire and talks with Kabila.

Opposition spokesmen said as many as 462 of the assembly 738 members took part in the debate. Witnesses said a majority of those present approved the motion by acclamation, with some dissident Mobutu supporters voting with the opposition.
Supporters of Mobutu, most of whom boycotted the debate, have a majority in parliament. They said the vote fell short of a three-quarters majority needed to sack a prime minister.
In Nairobi, a spokeswoman for the U.N. World Food Programme said a plane carrying 35 tonnes of food was headed to Kisangani to help feed 40,000 displaced people.
She said rebels told Kisangani's residents they had two days to return looted aid agency food and since Tuesday sacks of food were left on roadsides in the city for aid workers to collect.
"It's pretty incredible. Once it has been looted we don't normally get it back," said spokeswoman Michele Quintaglie.
